bodyText:
What is a Computer Network?

A computer network is a group of two or more computers and other devices connected together so that they can communicate with each other and share resources. The connected devices are called nodes. A network allows users to share data, files, hardware such as printers and scanners, software, and internet access.

Data communication in a network means the exchange of data between two devices through a transmission medium, such as a cable or wireless signals. For communication to take place, the devices must follow a common set of rules, called a protocol. A protocol defines how data is formatted, transmitted, and received.

Basic Components of a Network

  • Sender and Receiver: The device that sends data is the sender, and the device that receives data is the receiver.

  • Message: The information or data to be communicated.

  • Transmission Medium: The physical or wireless path through which the message travels, for example twisted-pair cable, fibre-optic cable, or radio waves.

  • Protocol: The set of rules governing communication, for example TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol).

  • Network Devices: Hardware such as routers, switches, hubs, and modems that connect devices and direct data.

Why Networks Are Created

Networks are created mainly for resource sharing, communication, and reliability. Instead of buying a printer for every computer, one printer can be shared over a network. Networks also make communication faster through email, messaging, and video conferencing, and they allow data to be stored centrally and backed up more easily.

Historical Background

The first major computer network was ARPANET (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network), developed in the late 1960s by the United States Department of Defense's Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA). ARPANET became operational in 1969 and is regarded as the predecessor of the modern internet. In the 1970s, Vint Cerf and Robert Kahn developed TCP/IP, the protocol suite on which the internet still runs. On 1 January 1983, ARPANET officially adopted TCP/IP, a date often regarded as the birth of the internet.

bodyText:
Classification by Geographical Area

Networks are commonly classified by the geographical area they cover. The three main types are Local Area Network (LAN), Metropolitan Area Network (MAN), and Wide Area Network (WAN). A fourth type, the Personal Area Network (PAN), covers a very small area around a single person, such as Bluetooth connections between a phone and a headset.

Local Area Network (LAN)

A LAN connects computers within a small, limited area such as a home, office, school, or single building. It is usually owned, controlled, and maintained by a single organisation. LANs generally offer high data transfer speeds and low delay because the distances involved are short. The most common LAN technology is Ethernet, developed at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, with Robert Metcalfe as a key figure, and standardised as IEEE 802.3.

Metropolitan Area Network (MAN)

A MAN covers a larger area than a LAN, typically a city or a large campus. It connects several LANs together within that area. A MAN may be owned by a single organisation or by a group of organisations, and it is often operated by a telecommunications provider. An example is a cable television network or a city-wide network connecting the branches of a bank.

Wide Area Network (WAN)

A WAN covers a very large geographical area, such as a country, a continent, or the whole world. The internet is the largest example of a WAN. A WAN is not owned by a single organisation; it is formed by connecting many LANs and MANs through public communication links, satellites, and undersea cables. Because data travels over long distances, a WAN generally has lower speed and higher delay than a LAN.

Key Distinction for Exams

The main differences among LAN, MAN, and WAN are geographical coverage, ownership, speed, and cost. LAN covers the smallest area and is the fastest and cheapest to maintain; WAN covers the largest area and is the most expensive and slowest in relative terms; MAN lies between the two in both coverage and performance.

MAN stands for Metropolitan Area Network.
WAN stands for Wide Area Network.
PAN stands for Personal Area Network.

bodyText:
Why Network Devices Are Needed

Computers cannot form a useful network by cables alone. Network devices connect computers, direct data to the correct destination, and link one network to another. Each device works at a different level and performs a different job. Examiners commonly test the difference between a hub, a switch, a router, and a modem.

Hub

A hub is the simplest networking device. It connects several computers in a network and, when it receives data on one port, it broadcasts that data to all other ports. Every connected device receives the data, but only the intended recipient accepts it. A hub works at the Physical Layer (Layer 1) of the OSI model. Because it sends data everywhere, a hub creates unnecessary traffic and is less secure and less efficient than a switch. Hubs are now largely obsolete.

Switch

A switch also connects several devices within a network, but unlike a hub it learns the address of each connected device and forwards data only to the intended recipient. It uses the MAC (Media Access Control) address of devices to make forwarding decisions. A switch works at the Data Link Layer (Layer 2) of the OSI model. Because it sends data only where it is needed, a switch is faster, more efficient, and more secure than a hub.

Router

A router connects two or more different networks, for example a home network to the internet. It reads the IP (Internet Protocol) address of data packets and chooses the best path for them to reach their destination. A router works at the Network Layer (Layer 3) of the OSI model. It also assigns local IP addresses in a home network and separates one network from another, which improves security.

Modem

A modem connects a computer or a local network to the internet through a telephone line, cable line, or fibre connection. The word modem is short for modulator-demodulator. Modulation converts digital signals from a computer into analogue signals suitable for transmission over a telephone line, and demodulation converts incoming analogue signals back into digital signals. A modem is therefore needed where the communication line carries analogue signals but the computer works with digital signals.

bodyText:
The Internet

The internet is a global network of interconnected computer networks that communicate using the TCP/IP protocol suite. It is public: anyone with an internet connection can access its public services, such as websites, email, and search engines. The World Wide Web (WWW), invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 at CERN, is a service that runs on the internet; the web and the internet are not the same thing. The internet has no single owner and no central control.

The Intranet

An intranet is a private network within an organisation that uses internet technologies, such as web browsers and web servers, but is accessible only to authorised members of that organisation, for example its employees. It is used to share internal documents, announcements, policies, and applications securely. An intranet is protected from the public internet by a firewall and by login credentials.

The Extranet

An extranet is an extension of an organisation's intranet that allows controlled access to selected outside users, such as business partners, suppliers, customers, or clients. For example, a company may give a supplier extranet access to check stock levels or place orders, without giving access to its full internal network. An extranet therefore sits between a fully private intranet and the fully public internet.

Key Distinction for Exams

The difference lies in who may access the network. The internet is open to the public, an intranet is restricted to members of one organisation, and an extranet is restricted to one organisation plus its authorised external partners. All three use the same underlying internet technologies, but their access rules and purposes differ.
keyPoints: The internet is a global network of interconnected networks that communicate using TCP/IP.
The internet is public and has no single owner.
The World Wide Web (WWW) is a service that runs on the internet; the web and the internet are not the same thing.
The World Wide Web was invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 at CERN.
An intranet is a private network within one organisation that uses internet technologies.
An intranet is accessible only to authorised members of the organisation, such as its employees.
An intranet is protected from the public internet by a firewall and login credentials.
An extranet is an extension of an intranet that gives controlled access to selected outside users.
Typical extranet users are business partners, suppliers, and customers.
The internet is open to the public, an intranet is restricted to one organisation, and an extranet is open to one organisation plus its authorised partners.
A firewall is a security system that controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on security rules.
All three — internet, intranet, and extranet — use the same underlying internet technologies, but differ in access.
